title: The Gita at Walden
hookLine: he bathed his mind in the Bhagavad Gita and imagined Walden's water mingling with the Ganges (Walden 16)

lines: A POND AND A FAR RIVER.
cards: What could a small New England pond have to do with a river on the other side of the earth?
In the winter Thoreau describes, an ice company came to Walden with horses, saws and long tools, cutting the frozen pond into blocks and stacking them high on the shore.
The ice would be shipped, he tells us, to hot cities a world away. He watched them work. Then he went back to his cabin, his book and his well.
And somewhere between the ice saws and the bucket, an answer arrived.

teach.b: First, the book. Near the end of The Pond in Winter, Thoreau tells us what he reads in the morning: "In the morning I bathe my intellect in the stupendous and cosmogonal philosophy of the Bhagvat Geeta."
That's his spelling of the Bhagavad Gita, the Hindu scripture where Krishna counsels the warrior Arjuna, whose dropped bow you met on day seven hundred twenty-four. Notice the verb.
Not study, not skim: bathe, the way you'd step into the pond. Second, the well.
He puts down the book and goes to his well for water, and there, in his imagination, he meets the servant of a Brahmin priest who sits in his temple on the Ganges reading the Vedas.
They draw water, he says, from the same well, and their buckets grate together. A scripture read at dawn has turned a chore into a meeting. Third, the ice.

Thoreau thinks of the blocks cut from Walden and shipped to hot cities in India, among other places, and writes: "The pure Walden water is mingled with the sacred water of the Ganges." It's a picture of water traveling.
It's also ideas traveling the other way, from the Ganges to a cabin in Massachusetts. Fourth, what he's doing. Thoreau doesn't claim the Gita as his, or say what Hindus should make of it.

He treats it as a neighbor's well he's been allowed to drink from. A line from far away came into his ordinary morning and changed the size of it. His small pond, read beside a great river, didn't feel small anymore.

how: Hindus read the Bhagavad Gita as scripture; Thoreau, writing as a reader from outside the tradition, describes bathing his mind in it each morning and picturing Walden's water mingling with the Ganges.

Walden's water mingling with the sacred water of the Ganges.

games.why: he pictured the waters meeting, and at his own well, a Brahmin's servant drawing water beside him.

practice: Bring to mind one line from a tradition, a land or a language far from your own: something you've heard on this path, or something a friend once said that came from their grandmother's world.
If nothing comes, borrow Thoreau's: the pure Walden water is mingled with the sacred water of the Ganges. Let the line sit in you like water, without analyzing it, a morning bath.

wordCard.voice: The Gita at Walden. Thoreau bathed his mind in the Bhagavad Gita in the mornings, and pictured his pond's water mingling with the Ganges. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit, from the Hindu tradition: the Bhagavad Gita, rendered in English as 'the song of the Lord'. Thoreau spelled it Bhagvat Geeta.

carryVoice: Your line: the Ganges and Walden. A far line can live inside an ordinary morning. Same time tomorrow.
